lesson.title: Place Value in Base 60
lesson.objective: Read and write whole numbers in base 60, and convert between base 60 and base 10 using place values of 1, 60, and 3600.
lesson.approachReason: Fully worked conversions establish the procedure, then progressively less-supported tasks let the learner apply it independently.

blocks.heading: Two groups, one number
blocks.problem:
Suppose a number has two base-60 groups: 2 on the left and 15 on the right. We will write this as **[2, 15]**, using modern brackets and commas to make the groups clear—not reproducing Babylonian writing.

The rightmost group counts ones. The next group counts sixties. What is this number in base 10?

steps.title: Read the places
steps.text: The 2 means two sixties; the 15 means fifteen ones.
steps.why: A group's position tells you how much each unit in that group is worth.

steps.title: Find each contribution
steps.why: Multiply each group by its place value.

steps.title: Combine them
steps.why: Add the contributions to get the base-10 value.

blocks.heading: One group can hold up to 59
blocks.body:
In base 10, each digit has a value from 0 to 9. In base 60, each **place-value group** has a value from 0 to 59—even when we need two decimal digits to write that value.

Once a group reaches 60, it becomes one unit in the place to its left. Our commas separate places: [2, 15] has two places, not three.
blocks.example:
[1, 59] = 60 + 59 = 119.

Adding one gives [2, 0] = 120: sixty ones have become another sixty.

hints: Label the right-hand place first, then the place to its left.
Find the value of the full bundles before adding the individual items.
blocks.retry: Treat the comma as a boundary between places. The left group counts bundles of sixty, while the right group counts individual items.

blocks.heading: Your turn: turn groups into a total
blocks.prompt:
Convert **[3, 25]** from base 60 to base 10.

Complete the calculation: \(3\times60+25=\ ?\)

traps.feedback: This joins the written groups instead of weighting them by their places.
This adds the group values without accounting for the sixties place.

hints: First calculate the value of three sixties.
blocks.solution: The left group contributes 3 × 60 = 180. The right group contributes 25, so 180 + 25 = 205.

blocks.heading: Go the other way
blocks.problem: Write the base-10 number **194** in base 60. We need to find how many full groups of sixty it contains, then how many ones remain.

steps.title: Find full sixties
steps.text: 3 × 60 = 180, while 4 × 60 = 240. So 194 contains three full sixties.
steps.why: Choose the largest whole number of sixties that does not exceed the total.

steps.title: Find what remains
steps.why: These fourteen remaining units belong in the ones place.

steps.title: Write and verify
steps.why: The remainder is below 60, so it fits in one group.

hints: How many full sixties fit into the total?
Check both the value of your representation and the size of each group.
blocks.retry: A valid group is less than 60. If a proposed ones group is 60 or more, another full sixty must move into the place to its left.

blocks.heading: Another step left means ×60 again
blocks.body:
The place values grow by a factor of 60 as you move left: **1, 60, 3600**, because \(60\times60=3600\). Read a three-group number by multiplying each group by its place value and adding.

In our modern notation, 0 keeps an empty place visible. In [1, 0, 5], the middle place is empty, but the leftmost 1 still counts 3600.
blocks.example:
[1, 0, 5] = 1 × 3600 + 0 × 60 + 5 = 3605.

[1, 5] = 1 × 60 + 5 = 65.

Removing an empty place changes the value.

blocks.heading: Read three places
blocks.prompt: Convert **[1, 2, 5]** from base 60 to base 10. Work from the rightmost place to identify the weight of each group.

traps.feedback: This gives both left-hand groups a weight of 60. Each step left must multiply the weight by another 60.
This reads the groups as decimal digits rather than using base-60 place values.

hints: Start with 1 on the right, then multiply the place value by 60 at each step left.
Calculate the three contributions separately before adding.
blocks.solution: The places are 3600, 60, and 1 from left to right. Therefore 1 × 3600 + 2 × 60 + 5 = 3600 + 120 + 5 = 3725.

hints: Label all three positions, starting at the right.
The zero changes one contribution to zero; it does not remove a position.
blocks.retry: An empty middle place contributes nothing, but still separates the ones place from the 3600s place. Count positions, including the zero, before calculating.

activities.title: Write 267 in base 60
activities.prompt: Arrange these steps to convert the base-10 number 267 into a two-group base-60 number.
activities.reveal: 267 contains four full sixties and 27 remaining ones: 4 × 60 + 27 = 240 + 27 = 267. Its base-60 form is [4, 27].
steps: Find the number of full sixties: 4 × 60 = 240, but 5 × 60 = 300 is too much.
Put 4 in the sixties place and 27 in the ones place: [4, 27].

questions.question: In an illustrative inventory, a clerk records a count as [4, 8] in our base-60 notation. What count should you enter in a base-10 spreadsheet?
questions.explanation: The 4 counts sixties and the 8 counts ones: 4 × 60 + 8 = 240 + 8 = 248.

questions.question: A workshop has 182 beads. Using groups valued from 0 to 59, what two-group base-60 record should it write?
questions.explanation: 182 = 3 × 60 + 2, so the record is [3, 2]. Although 2 × 60 + 62 also totals 182, 62 is too large for a single group.

questions.question: A museum activity labels a quantity [1, 0, 12] in our modern base-60 notation. What base-10 quantity does the label represent?
questions.explanation: All three positions count, including the empty middle one: 1 × 3600 + 0 × 60 + 12 = 3612. Removing the zero would move the 1 into a different place.

problems: The ordering activity supplies every calculation and the final representation, so it tests recognition of a procedure more than independent conversion.
Practice in writing base-60 numbers stops at two places, although the objective includes conversions using the 3600 place.
Check retries mostly repeat the original place-value explanation rather than offering a genuinely different explanation or representation.
The final check closely mirrors the worked example with an empty middle place, limiting transfer beyond the demonstrated pattern.
